ket_qua.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote covers roughly one hectare, about the size of two soccer fields.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: National Geographic (2017) says about one hectare, roughly two soccer fields (about 12,000 sq yd); Radio Nacional and Voz de América say just over one hectare. Other estimates range from 1.2 ha (El Pais via Wikipedia) to 1.57 ha (Red Prensa Verde), so 'roughly' is appropriate.

ket_qua.statement: Media reports often describe Santa Cruz del Islote as one of the most densely populated islands in the world; the claim depends on population estimates that vary widely.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: NatGeo, CNN, The Guardian, BBC Mundo and others call it the most crowded or densely populated island; population figures in reputable outlets range from about 500 to 1,300, and the DANE census counted 432 in 2018, so the hedge is needed.

ket_qua.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote is surrounded by larger islands of the San Bernardo archipelago, such as Múcura and Tintipán, which have beaches and vegetation including mangroves.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Tintipán is the largest island in the archipelago and its interior is mangrove swamp; Múcura has the only public beach plus hotel beaches and remaining mangroves (Red Prensa Verde); BBC Mundo notes both have water and farmland.

ket_qua.statement: According to a story told by locals, the fishermen who first settled on Santa Cruz del Islote chose it because it had no mosquitoes.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: CNN (Spanish edition) reports the legend that fishermen stayed after finding no mosquitoes; BBC Mundo says residents cite the absence of mosquitoes as a key reason the settlers built there; Radio Nacional tells the same story about the jején. All present it as local lore.

ket_qua.statement: The boat ride from Cartagena to Santa Cruz del Islote takes about two hours, longer in rough seas; reported times vary.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: About two hours from Cartagena: National Geographic (2017), Noticias RCN (2023), Radio Nacional, BBC Mundo (2018) and La Nación (2026, 'unas dos horas'). Variation is real but only weakly sourced: booking sites list 2 h to 2 h 30 by operator, and a travel guide (kimkim) says the crossing is 'usually quite bumpy, depending on sea conditions'. No official source states that rough seas lengthen the trip, so that part rests on travel sites; the hedge in the narration ('a couple of hours, more if the sea is rough') is reasonable.

ket_qua.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote is roughly 45 minutes to an hour by small motorboat (lancha) from Tolú, on Colombia's Caribbean coast; sources differ.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: ProColombia's official tourism site (Colombia Travel) says 45 minutes by lancha from Tolú; Noticias RCN (2023), Voz de América, Radio Nacional and BBC Mundo (2018) all say about one hour. The 45-60 minute range with 'sources differ' matches what the sources say; keep the hedge.

ket_qua.statement: Santa Cruz del Islote has more than a hundred houses (Colombia's 2018 census counted 120 dwellings), a school, a restaurant and a small square with a cross that gives the island its name, and no cars.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Primary source: the Consejo de Estado ruling (acción popular 25000-23-24-000-2012-00278-03) quotes DANE's reply that the 2018 CNPV counted 120 viviendas, 96 hogares and 432 people in Santa Cruz del Islote. BBC Mundo (2018) says 'más de un centenar de viviendas' (press counts range from 97 in NatGeo 2017 to 140-150 in VOA and RCN). School (VOA, BBC Mundo, RCN), a restaurant (VOA), the cement cross that gave the island its name (NatGeo), no roads (NatGeo) and 'no circulan autos ni motos' (La Nación 2026) are all supported.

ket_qua.ghi_chu: ABC Economía (5 Mar 2019): 'La Fundación Pintuco, junto con la Armada Nacional, pintó todas las fachadas' and 'nueve murales en co-creación con la comunidad'. It is the only source found (likely based on a press release); no Pintuco or Navy page was found.

ket_qua.statement: Fishing and tourism are the two pillars of the economy of Santa Cruz del Islote; tourism is becoming increasingly important.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: Re-checked 2026-11-26 for the revised wording. Two pillars: Radio Nacional says the island 'vive esencialmente del turismo y la pesca'; Voz de América (8 Aug 2023): 'La mayoría de ellos se dedica al turismo y a la pesca' and 'Santa Cruz del Islote vive del turismo y de la pesca'; BBC Mundo (2018): most residents 'viven de la pesca o el turismo'. Increasingly important: La Nación (31 Jul 2026) says 'El turismo está cobrando un rol cada vez más protagónico en la economía de Santa Cruz del Islote', about 500 visitors land daily, and waste has become a bigger problem 'con el crecimiento del turismo', while 'su principal sustento sigue siendo la pesca'. Radio Nacional also mentions a rising number of people on the island. Only La Nación states the trend explicitly, but no source contradicts it; the revised wording no longer overstates it the way 'growing fast' did. Los Andes (2024) was blocked (403) and the CNN Travel page returned 451.

ket_qua.ghi_chu: Guardian article by Iñigo Alexander (2023), read via syndicated copies because theguardian.com was blocked: islands 'at an average of only 2 metres (6ft) above the waterline'; on Santa Cruz del Islote residents wake to wet floors and homes can flood at any time (der Freitag). ket_qua.statement: A 2014 local government report, cited by The Guardian, found erosion affecting about 45% of the San Bernardo archipelago's coastlines; the small nearby island of Maravilla has since disappeared.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: The Guardian (2023, read via der Freitag's translation; inkl returned 403 and the Island Innovation copy is truncated) cites a 2014 report by the local administration on 45% of San Bernardo's coasts, and says Maravilla has been gone since 2017. Red Prensa Verde confirms Maravilla, a San Bernardo islet of under one hectare (Invemar: 0.004 km2) used by the Islote community, no longer exists, though the date is unclear: about 2017 (community), 2006-2007 (Invemar citing Parques Nacionales), from 2015 (a researcher). 'Has since', meaning after 2014, follows the Guardian; the narration gives no date, which is the safe choice. The 2014 report itself could not be opened.

ket_qua.statement: Global sea levels are expected to rise by up to about 30 cm (about one foot) by 2050.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: IPCC AR6 likely range for 2050 global mean sea level rise relative to 1995-2014 is 0.15-0.23 m (SSP1-1.9) up to 0.20-0.29 m (SSP5-8.5), so 'up to about 30 cm' is the top of the range. NOAA's 25-30 cm figure applies to US coastlines, not the globe.

ket_qua.statement: Students from Santa Cruz del Islote who want to continue beyond the island's school must leave the island.
ket_qua.ghi_chu: National Geographic (2017): the island's school runs through tenth grade, and students who want to keep learning 'must either commute to schools off of the island or leave their home entirely'. Radio Nacional adds that after bachillerato there are few chances to go to university. Commuting still means leaving the island, so 'must leave' holds; the school's top grade may have changed since 2017, and the narration does not state it.
